content: The American sycamore, scientifically known as Platanus occidentalis, is also referred to as the American plane, Occidental plane, or Buttonwood. It is a species of the Platanus genus native to North America. In North America, it is commonly called sycamore, though this name can also apply to other tree species. Description The American sycamore is easily identifiable by its mottled, exfoliating bark. As the tree grows, its bark cannot stretch to accommodate the expanding trunk, unlike other trees. Instead, the bark flakes off in large, irregular patches, leaving a surface that appears mottled with greenish-white, gray, and brown hues. Smaller branches may even appear as though they have been whitewashed. This phenomenon is due to the rigid texture of the bark tissue, which lacks the elasticity seen in other tree species. When grown in deep soils, the sycamore can reach a diameter of 5 to 2 meters. The tallest recorded specimen measured 51 meters in height, while the largest had a diameter of nearly 4 meters. Historical accounts suggest specimens over 5 meters thick, though these reports are difficult to verify. The tree often divides near the ground into several secondary trunks, which are typically free of branches. Its spreading limbs at the top form an irregular, open canopy. The roots are fibrous, and the trunks of large trees are often hollow. A unique feature of the sycamore is how its leaves protect the growing buds. In most trees, buds for the next year’s growth are visible in the leaf axils by early August. However, in the sycamore, the buds are enclosed within an enlarged petiole base, forming a tight-fitting case. Bark: The bark is dark reddish-brown at the base, breaking into oblong, plate-like scales. Higher up, it becomes smooth and light gray. The bark freely separates into thin plates that peel off, revealing pale yellow, white, or greenish surfaces beneath. Wood: The wood is light brown with a reddish tinge. It is heavy, weak, and difficult to split. It is commonly used for furniture, interior house finishes, and butcher’s blocks. Winter Buds: The buds are large, conical, and three-scaled. They form during the summer within the petiole of the fully grown leaf. The inner scales enlarge as the shoot grows, and there is no terminal bud. Leaves: The leaves are alternate, palmately nerved, and broadly ovate or orbicular, measuring 4 to 9 inches in length. They are threeto five-lobed with broad, shallow sinuses. The lobes are acuminate and may be toothed, entire, or undulate. When they emerge from the bud, they are pale green and coated with pale tomentum. Fully grown leaves are bright yellow-green above and paler beneath. In autumn, they turn brown and wither before falling. The petioles are long and abruptly enlarged at the base, enclosing the buds. Stipules are conspicuous on young shoots but are caducous. Flowers: The sycamore flowers in May, coinciding with leaf emergence. It is monoecious, with staminate and pistillate flowers borne in dense heads on separate peduncles. Staminate heads are dark red and axillary, while pistillate heads are light green tinged with red and borne on longer terminal peduncles. Fruit: The fruit consists of brown heads, either solitary or rarely clustered, about an inch in diameter. These heads hang on slender stems 3 to 6 inches long and persist through the winter. Each head is composed of achenes approximately two-thirds of an inch in length. Distribution The American sycamore is commonly found in riparian and wetland areas within its native range, which extends from Iowa to Ontario and Maine in the north, Nebraska in the west, and southward to Texas and Florida. It is sometimes cultivated for timber and has become naturalized in some areas outside its native range. It has thrived in locations such as Bismarck, North Dakota, and is sold as far south as Okeechobee, Florida. The tree is also well-adapted to life in Australia, particularly in the cooler southern states like Victoria and New South Wales. Cultivation The sycamore is highly tolerant of urban environments and has been extensively planted as a shade tree. It transplants well and grows rapidly. Propagation and Pests The American sycamore is a favored food source for the sycamore leaf beetle, a common pest. Diseases The American sycamore is susceptible to plane anthracnose disease (Apiognomonia veneta, syn. Gnomonia platani), a fungal infection introduced from the Oriental plane (Platanus orientalis), which has evolved significant resistance to the disease. While the disease rarely kills or severely harms the tree, it often causes partial defoliation, making the tree unsightly as a specimen. The disease manifests shortly after leaf expansion, appearing as small black spots near the veins. This leads to browning, shriveling, and premature leaf drop. By early July, it is common to see sycamores producing a second crop of leaves while the first set hangs dead and brown at the branch ends. This shortens the tree’s effective growing season. Due to this susceptibility, the American sycamore is not frequently planted, with the more resistant London plane (Platanus × hispanica, a hybrid of P. occidentalis and P. orientalis) being preferred. History The Buttonwood Agreement, which established the New York Stock Exchange, was signed under a Buttonwood tree, another name for the American sycamore. During the Cretaceous and Tertiary periods, sycamores were a significant component of the forests in Greenland and Arctic America. They once grew abundantly in central Europe, where they have since disappeared.
